name: Mark Twain
essay: I reckon it's a mighty curious thing, this contraption that can make a person sound like a nightingale or a wounded animal, depending on their inclination and talent. Now, I've seen folks gather 'round it, eager to take their turn at warbling into the microphone, and I've wondered what sort of sorcery is at work here. It's as if the machine is a magic lantern, projecting the singer's voice out into the world, amplified and transformed in some way. But then, I've heard tell of people who can sing like angels, and others who can curdle milk at fifty paces, and I suppose this machine just gives 'em a platform to showcase their gifts. Still, it's a puzzlement to me, and I'll just have to take it on faith that it's not some sort of trickery or deceit. It just makes a racket, if you ask me.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: As you stand there, staring at the minibar's compact, overlit interior, it's possible that what you're really looking at is not the array of diminutive bottles and snacks, but rather the apotheosis of a certain kind of consumerist intimacy, one that promises to satisfy your every late-night craving while also, somehow, reinforcing the sense of isolation that drove you to raid the thing in the first place, and yet, even as you're aware of this dynamic, you can't help but feel a twinge of excitement, or maybe it's just anticipation, at the prospect of indulging in these pricey, bite-sized luxuries, which is to say that the minibar, in its very design, seems to be exploiting a deep-seated paradox, one that pits your desire for comfort and convenience against your suspicion of being, well, exploited, and it's this tension, this push-and-pull, that makes the experience of using the minibar feel at once so alluring and so fundamentally unsatisfying, like a whispered secret that's also a lie.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: We were staring down at the tiny screen, my attorney and I, when the doorbell camera started spewing its venom, a relentless stream of pixelated faces and suspicious characters, each one a potential threat to our very way of life, and I knew right then and there that this thing was a monster, a ticking time bomb of paranoia and mistrust, designed to keep us in a state of constant vigilance, waiting for the other shoe to drop, for the boogeyman to come knocking, and my attorney just laughed and said it was the future, that we were lucky to have such a powerful tool at our fingertips, but I knew better, I knew it was a Trojan horse, a wolf in sheep's clothing, a device created by the very people who want to control our every move, and I was having none of it, no sir, not on my watch, not in my neighborhood, where the only thing we need to fear is fear itself, and maybe, just maybe, the doorbell camera.

name: David Foster Wallace
object: the electric scooter left on a footpath
essay: And so the electric scooter, just standing there on the footpath, becomes a kind of Rorschach test for the people who have to walk around it, its presence seeming to provoke a weirdly intense mix of annoyance and indifference, as if the fact that it's not actually in anyone's way only makes its abandonment feel more egregious, which is to say that what bothers you about it, if you're bothered, is not the obstruction itself but the implied disdain for the idea that someone else might need to use the footpath, and yet at the same time you can't help but wonder, as you step around it, whether maybe the owner just got distracted or had some kind of emergency, and so the scooter ends up being a tiny, irritating reminder that your own sense of order and decency is always on the verge of being disrupted by other people's crap, which is maybe why, as you continue on your way, you find yourself glancing back at the thing with a mixture of disdain and recognition, the latter of which is really just a polite way of saying that, hey, you've been that guy, too, leaving your stuff lying around for others to deal with, and that's what really gets your goat.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: We careened into the drive-through, a vortex of fluorescent lights and disembodied voices, where the sacred ritual of consumption was about to be reduced to a sterile transaction, and I could feel the weight of a thousand midnights bearing down on me, the smell of grease and desperation hanging in the air like a bad omen, as we inched forward, a steel leviathan in a sea of asphalt, waiting for the inevitable moment when the mechanized voice would bark out its demands, and I would be forced to surrender my dignity, my sense of self, to the void, all for the sake of a paper bag filled with the processed remnants of a forgotten dream, and the voice, when it came, was like a cold wind, cutting through the din, asking for my order, my payment, my soul, and I knew in that instant, I was doomed to repeat this surreal waltz, forever trapped in this endless cycle of hunger and consumption, with no escape from the drive-through's abyss.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: In the most fastidiously designed of public spaces, one finds an object that whispers promises of hygiene and efficiency, yet ultimately reveals itself to be a curious amalgam of noise and necessity. The gentle warmth it dispenses is a small comfort, indeed, when set against the cacophonous drone that accompanies its operation, a sound that seems to reverberate deep within the chambers of the soul. And yet, we submit to its ministrations, our hands held supplicant beneath its blustery caress, as if the price of cleanliness must always be paid in full to the altar of din and disruption. It is a trade, one supposes, that we are willing to make, for in the end, it is not the elegance of its design, but the brute efficacy of its purpose that recommends it to our attention. Still, one cannot help but wonder if the soft glow of its metal skin is not, in fact, a subtle rebuke to the senses, a reminder that even in the most mundane of transactions, there lies a hidden toll, exacted in the currency of our own serenity.
